plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 28: Magnetic Forces and Fields
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional illustration of a positively charged particle following a helical path in a uniform magnetic field. Three axes meet at the origin O, with x running to the right, y upward, and z toward the lower left, and a small orange sphere labeled q sits at the origin. From the particle, a green arrow labeled 'v perp' points straight up along y, a short arrow labeled 'v para' points along the x direction, and a green arrow labeled 'v' between the two gives the total velocity. A blue arrow labeled with a vector B lies along the positive x-axis, and a red arrow labeled 'F' is drawn at the particle. An orange helix of roughly three turns occupies the right side of the frame, each loop circling in the plane perpendicular to x with small arrowheads on the coils marking the sense of rotation, and successive loops shifted steadily in the positive x direction. Above the coils a short green double-headed arrow labeled 'v para' spans the gap between two consecutive turns. Splitting the velocity into two components makes visible which part bends the trajectory and which part carries the particle forward. The drawing shows how a velocity oblique to the field yields circular motion superposed on uniform travel along it.

y-axis arrow pointing up with label 'y'
z-axis arrow pointing toward lower-left (out of screen) with label 'z'
origin marker labeled 'O' where the three axes meet
small orange sphere labeled 'q' at the origin (the charged particle)
green arrow labeled 'v_perp' pointing straight up along +y from the particle
green arrow labeled 'v_para' pointing along +x from the particle (short)
green arrow labeled 'v' (total velocity) diagonal between v_perp and v_para
blue arrow labeled 'B' lying along the positive x-axis
red arrow labeled 'F' at the particle pointing toward the helix axis (centripetal)
orange helix of ~3 turns centered on the x-axis, each loop in the y-z plane, shifted steadily in +x
small orange arrowheads on the helix coils marking the sense of gyration
green double-headed arrow labeled 'v_para' above the coils spanning the axial gap between two consecutive turns (the pitch)

interactions.label: Particle motion
interactions.teaches: Watching the charge trace the helix makes the superposition concrete: the perpendicular velocity component bends the path into a circle in the plane normal to B, while the parallel component carries the whole circle steadily along the field line

interactions.label: v_parallel (along B)
interactions.teaches: Increasing the velocity component along B stretches the spacing (pitch) between successive turns while the loop radius stays exactly the same, showing that forward speed alone sets how far the particle advances per gyration

interactions.label: v_perp (across B)
interactions.teaches: Changing the perpendicular component widens or shrinks the circular radius and the gyration speed while the axial advance per turn is untouched, revealing that only the cross-field velocity controls the orbit around the field line

demo_steps.title: Default helix
demo_steps.narration: With v_perp=1.0 and v_parallel=0.25 the charge follows a moderate helix: a fixed-radius circle in the y-z plane drifting along +x. The red F always points inward, supplying the centripetal force.

demo_steps.title: Stretch the pitch
demo_steps.narration: Raise v_parallel to 0.8. The loops spread far apart along x while their radius is unchanged — a faster parallel component means more travel per turn.

demo_steps.title: Widen the orbit
demo_steps.narration: Reset v_parallel to 0.25 and raise v_perp to 1.4. The circular radius grows and the gyration quickens, but the axial spacing between turns stays the same as in the first step.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: axes span roughly x in [0,6], y in [-2.5,2.5], z in [-2.5,2.5]; origin O at (0,0,0). Choose units m=q=B=1 so gyroradius r = v_perp (world units) and cyclotron frequency omega = 1; axial advance per radian = v_para, so pitch per full turn = 2*pi*v_para. Particle position: x(t)=v_para*t, y(t)=r*cos(omega*t), z(t)=r*sin(omega*t). At the illustrated instant the perpendicular velocity is along +y, so v_perp arrow points +y, v_para arrow points +x, total v is their diagonal sum in the x-y plane, and F = q(v x B) lies in the y-z plane pointing toward the x-axis (centripetal). Helix drawn as ~3 turns starting near the origin extending +x. Colors: sphere & helix orange #ff7f2a, velocity vectors green #3a9e3a, B blue #1f6fd6, F red #cc2222, axes black #111111. The green double-headed pitch marker sits above the coils at y ~ r+0.4 spanning one pitch in x.
interactionPlan.notes: Three.js: build the helix as a parametric THREE.Line (or TubeGeometry) regenerated whenever vParallel or vPerp changes; keep ~300 segments for smoothness. The animation advances a parameter t each frame and repositions the orange sphere, then recomputes the three velocity arrows (v_perp tangential in y-z plane, v_para along +x, v their sum) and F = normalize(cross(v,B)) scaled, all anchored at the moving particle. Add small cone arrowheads on the coil to show gyration sense. Keep both sliders and the animation live simultaneously so the learner sees radius/pitch respond in real time.

authoredContext:
The result is a helical motion, as shown in the following figure.

A charged particle moving with a velocity not in the same direction as the magnetic field. The velocity component perpendicular to the magnetic field creates circular motion, whereas the component of the velocity parallel to the field moves the particle along a straight line. The pitch is the horizontal distance between two consecutive circles. The resulting motion is helical.

An illustration of a positively charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field. The field is in the positive x direction. The initial velocity is shown as having a component, v sub para, in the positive x direction and another component, v sub perp, in the positive y direction. The particle moves in a helix that loops in the y z plane (counterclockwise from the particle’s perspective) and advances in the positive x direction.

While the charged particle travels in a helical path, it may enter a region where the magnetic field is not uniform. In particular, suppose a particle travels from a region of strong magnetic field to a region of weaker field, then back to a region of stronger field. The particle may reflect back before entering the stronger magnetic field region. This is similar to a wave on a string traveling from a very light, thin string to a hard wall and reflecting backward. If the reflection happens at both ends, the particle is trapped in a so-called magnetic bottle.

demo_steps.title: Default helix
demo_steps.narration: With v_perp=1.0 and v_parallel=0.25 the charge follows a moderate helix: a fixed-radius circle in the y-z plane drifting along +x. The red F always points inward, supplying the centripetal force.

demo_steps.title: Stretch the pitch
demo_steps.narration: Raise v_parallel to 0.8. The loops spread far apart along x while their radius is unchanged — a faster parallel component means more travel per turn.

demo_steps.title: Widen the orbit
demo_steps.narration: Reset v_parallel to 0.25 and raise v_perp to 1.4. The circular radius grows and the gyration quickens, but the axial spacing between turns stays the same as in the first step.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: axes span roughly x in [0,6], y in [-2.5,2.5], z in [-2.5,2.5]; origin O at (0,0,0). Choose units m=q=B=1 so gyroradius r = v_perp (world units) and cyclotron frequency omega = 1; axial advance per radian = v_para, so pitch per full turn = 2*pi*v_para. Particle position: x(t)=v_para*t, y(t)=r*cos(omega*t), z(t)=r*sin(omega*t). At the illustrated instant the perpendicular velocity is along +y, so v_perp arrow points +y, v_para arrow points +x, total v is their diagonal sum in the x-y plane, and F = q(v x B) lies in the y-z plane pointing toward the x-axis (centripetal). Helix drawn as ~3 turns starting near the origin extending +x. Colors: sphere & helix orange #ff7f2a, velocity vectors green #3a9e3a, B blue #1f6fd6, F red #cc2222, axes black #111111. The green double-headed pitch marker sits above the coils at y ~ r+0.4 spanning one pitch in x.
interactionPlan.notes: Three.js: build the helix as a parametric THREE.Line (or TubeGeometry) regenerated whenever vParallel or vPerp changes; keep ~300 segments for smoothness. The animation advances a parameter t each frame and repositions the orange sphere, then recomputes the three velocity arrows (v_perp tangential in y-z plane, v_para along +x, v their sum) and F = normalize(cross(v,B)) scaled, all anchored at the moving particle. Add small cone arrowheads on the coil to show gyration sense. Keep both sliders and the animation live simultaneously so the learner sees radius/pitch respond in real time.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure is a three-dimensional illustration of a positively charged particle following a helical path in a uniform magnetic field. Three axes meet at the origin O, with x running to the right, y upward, and z toward the lower left, and a small orange sphere labeled q sits at the origin. From the particle, a green arrow labeled 'v perp' points straight up along y, a short arrow labeled 'v para' points along the x direction, and a green arrow labeled 'v' between the two gives the total velocity. A blue arrow labeled with a vector B lies along the positive x-axis, and a red arrow labeled 'F' is drawn at the particle. An orange helix of roughly three turns occupies the right side of the frame, each loop circling in the plane perpendicular to x with small arrowheads on the coils marking the sense of rotation, and successive loops shifted steadily in the positive x direction. Above the coils a short green double-headed arrow labeled 'v para' spans the gap between two consecutive turns. Splitting the velocity into two components makes visible which part bends the trajectory and which part carries the particle forward. The drawing shows how a velocity oblique to the field yields circular motion superposed on uniform travel along it.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- Animation for particle motion: the learner starts the simulation, the charged particle circles while advancing along the magnetic-field axis, showing that perpendicular velocity creates rotation and parallel velocity creates translation.
- Slider for v_parallel: the learner increases the component along B, the helix pitch stretches while the loop radius stays fixed, clarifying how forward speed sets spacing between turns.
- Slider for v_perp: the learner changes the perpendicular component, the circular radius and rotation speed update while axial advance is unchanged, showing which velocity component controls the gyration around the field line.
